title: 2 John
subtitle: a short letter about love, truth and an open door
lead: 2 John has fewer verses than any other book of the Bible: thirteen. A writer who calls himself only "the Elder" writes to "the chosen lady and her children," a church or a Christian family, whom he loves "in truth." He is glad that some of them are walking in truth, and he reminds them of the command they had from the beginning: love each other.

Then he warns them. Many deceivers have gone out into the world who "do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh." If one of them comes, the readers must not take him into the house or even say "Greetings!" to him. The letter is a window on the first churches: Christians met in homes, teachers traveled from house to house, and the door of a house church was where truth was kept or lost. It is also a hard saying that churches have argued over ever since.
facts: "The Elder" (1:1), traditionally John the apostle; some early writers, and some scholars today, think of another John, "John the Elder," or a leader of the circle that produced John's Gospel and letters. The same man wrote 3 John.
Uncertain. Most proposals fall between the 60s and about AD 110; many scholars place the three letters of John close together around AD 90-110, after the Gospel.
Churches meeting in houses, in tradition the churches around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, visited by traveling teachers
A short letter in the usual form of its day: greeting, cause for joy, request, warning, hope of a visit, greetings
Greek, simple and repetitive, very close to 1 John
1 chapter, 13 verses (245 words in the SBL Greek text), the fewest verses of any book of the Bible
1 John (the same teaching about love, truth and the antichrist) and 3 John (the same writer, opening and ending)
authorship: The apostle John wrote it in old age at Ephesus, calling himself "the Elder" because everyone knew who he was. Irenaeus (about 180) quotes it as the teaching of John, the Lord's disciple, though once he cites it as if it were part of 1 John. Clement of Alexandria wrote a comment on it about 200.

Papias, early in the 100s, spoke of "the presbyter John" as well as the apostle. Eusebius (about 325) took this to mean two Johns in Asia, and passed on the report of others that two tombs at Ephesus were each called John's (Church History 3.39.5-6). He listed 2 and 3 John among the disputed books, unsure "whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name." Jerome (392) reports that many gave these two letters to John the presbyter. Some scholars today hold this view.

Most scholars think the same person wrote 2 and 3 John, and that 2 John is closely tied to 1 John, whose phrases it repeats. Whether he also wrote 1 John and the Gospel, or belonged to a circle (a "Johannine school") that did, is debated; a minority doubt that one man wrote 2 and 3 John, and Rudolf Bultmann held that 2 John was a forgery based on 3 John. Plummer argued from the bare title: "the Elder" is "a designation which a writer personating S. John would scarcely have chosen, as being too indistinct," while an elder who was not posing as the apostle "would hardly call himself 'The Elder.'"

audience.to: "The chosen lady and her children" (1:1): most likely a church in the Elder's care, pictured as a woman, with its members as her children, though some take her to be a Christian woman who led a household, perhaps one where a church met. Her "chosen sister" (1:13) is the church or family where the Elder is. The readers met in a house and received traveling teachers who stayed with them and taught them. Some of their "children" were walking in truth (1:4).
audience.why: Teachers who "do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh" (1:7) were traveling among the churches, perhaps the same people who had left the church of 1 John (1 John 2:19). The Elder writes to keep the lady's house from becoming their base. He first reminds her of the command to love each other, so that the warning comes from love, and then tells her not to receive such teachers or greet them, since that would share in their work. Knowing the setting changes the reading: the rule is about a house church welcoming a teacher who would speak in its meeting, not about a family refusing kindness to a stranger at the door.
views: The lady is a congregation and her children its members; the sister is another church (Amos Wilder, for one, held that the letter's content shows it was written to a whole church, not one person; Plummer leaves the question open).
A real Christian woman, perhaps named Kyria ("Lady"), whose household received traveling teachers (Ellicott's commentary; the Expositor's Bible).
Clement of Alexandria, in comments that survive only in a Latin translation (the Adumbrations): a "Babylonian lady, by name Electa"; Plummer answers that her sister is also "chosen."

outline: Greeting from the Elder to the chosen lady and her children, in truth and love
Joy at children walking in truth; the old command to love each other
Deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh; do not receive them or greet them
A visit hoped for; greetings from the chosen sister's children

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter in its world: house churches, traveling teachers who lived on their hosts' welcome, the rules of the Didache for testing them, the ordinary Greek letter on a sheet of papyrus, and Irenaeus' stories of John and Cerinthus at Ephesus.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks the scholars' questions: who "the Elder" was (the apostle, Papias' John the Elder, a leader of a Johannine circle), whether the lady is a church or a woman, how 2 John relates to 1 and 3 John, who the deceivers were, the date, the variants, and why the letter was long disputed.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the craft of a thirteen-verse letter: three key words (truth, love, command), the shift between "you" singular and plural, the play between "I was glad" and "Greetings!" (the same Greek verb), and the shared opening and ending with 3 John.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the Elder as a Jewish teacher: "walking" as the Hebrew way to speak of life (halakhah), the command received from the Father, Deuteronomy's test of a prophet who leads people off God's road (Deuteronomy 13), and the Hebrew idiom "mouth to mouth" behind 1:12 (Numbers 12:8; Jeremiah 32:4).

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Reads with the church: Irenaeus, Clement and the Council of Carthage of 256 on refusing heretics, and Rome's opposite ruling in that dispute; the long dispute over whether the letter belongs in the Bible; the readings of the chosen lady; and how the rule of 1:10-11 has been applied.

sections.b:
Read it aloud in under two minutes, as its first hearers did. Then read it beside 1 John and 3 John. With 1 John it shares its teaching: the old and new command (1 John 2:7-8), the antichrist (1 John 2:18-22), the confession that Jesus Christ came in the flesh (1 John 4:2-3), and joy made full (1 John 1:4). With 3 John it shares its writer, "the Elder," its opening ("whom I love in truth") and its ending ("paper and ink... face to face"). 1 John says what the truth is; 2 John tells a church not to open its door to those who deny it; 3 John shows a church shutting its door on the Elder's own people.

Watch three words: truth (five times), love (four) and command (four). The Elder holds them together. Love without truth would welcome anyone; truth without love would turn a church into a court. The notes mark where English hides the Greek: "the chosen lady" (1:1), "coming" in the flesh (1:7), "goes ahead" (1:9) and "Greetings!" (1:10).

sections.h: The Elder and the three letters of John
sections.b:
None of the three letters names its writer. 2 and 3 John call him "the Elder"; 1 John speaks as one of those who saw and heard the word of life. Irenaeus quotes 2 John as the teaching of John, the Lord's disciple, and in one place cites 2 John 7-8 as if it were part of 1 John (Against Heresies 3.16.8), a slip Plummer puts down to memory. Papias, quoted by Eusebius, names "the presbyter John" alongside the apostles, and Eusebius concluded that there were two Johns in Asia (Church History 3.39.4-6). Jerome says that in his day the last two letters were "said to be the work of John the presbyter" (Lives of Illustrious Men 9).

Most modern scholars agree that one man wrote 2 and 3 John and that he belonged to the same circle as 1 John and the Gospel of John; whether he was the apostle, the Elder of Papias or another leader is still argued. The topic page on John sets out the four Johns of the tradition. Since the letters say so little, the Plain follows the text: "the Elder."

sections.h: 2 John among the books of the Bible
sections.b:
2 John was known early but accepted slowly, probably because it is so short and private. Irenaeus quotes it about 180, Clement of Alexandria commented on it about 200, and the Muratorian list counts two letters "bearing the name of John" among those received in the church, without saying which two. Eusebius, about 325, wrote that 1 John was accepted without dispute, "but the other two are disputed," and placed "those that are called the second and third of John" among the disputed writings "which are nevertheless recognized by many" (Church History 3.24.17; 3.25.3). Athanasius' Easter letter of 367, the Synod of Hippo and the Council of Carthage (397) list all three letters of John.

The Syriac churches took longer. The Peshitta, the standard Syriac New Testament by the early 400s, left out 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation; the five were added in the Harklean version of 616. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles today all include 2 John. Lutheran theology kept Luther's distinction between books never disputed and the "antilegomena," the books once disputed, and current Lutheran usage counts 2 Peter, 2 John and 3 John among the antilegomena, while they remain in the Lutheran Bible. See the topic page on the canon.

The site translates the SBL Greek New Testament, but in the Catholic Letters (James to Jude) the 28th Nestle-Aland edition follows the Editio Critica Maior, the fullest modern edition, and the Plain follows that text where the two differ. In 2 John they differ at 1:12, where NA28 reads "our joy" and the SBL text "your joy." The other variants worth knowing are where the KJV reads differently: "the Lord Jesus Christ" (1:3, KJV), "are entered into the world" (1:7, KJV), "that we lose not those things which we have wrought" (1:8, KJV), "Whosoever transgresseth" and the second "of Christ" (1:9, KJV), "I trust to come unto you" (1:12, KJV), and the closing "Amen" (1:13, KJV). None changes the teaching of the letter.

spec.title: Claude's theory: "Babylonian" from 1 Peter
spec.body: This is my own guess. Clement of Alexandria says the letter was written "to a Babylonian lady, by name Electa." Nothing in 2 John mentions Babylon. But 1 Peter ends with greetings from a woman "in Babylon" who is "chosen together with" the readers (1 Peter 5:13, Greek hē en Babylōni syneklektē), a phrase most readers take as a church in Rome. A reader who knew both letters could join 2 John's "chosen lady" and "chosen sister" to 1 Peter's chosen one in Babylon, and so arrive at a "Babylonian" woman named "Chosen." I have not found this explanation in the sources I checked, and it remains a guess about where Clement's tradition came from.

prompts: A hand-drawn scroll scene in ink and earth colors: the doorway of a modest house in a Roman-era town of Asia, an older woman holding a small papyrus letter, children and adults gathered inside around a low table, and at the threshold a traveling teacher with a staff and bag, the woman's hand raised to stop him. Mixed style of ancient manuscript drawing, cave-art figures and modern line art, soft torn parchment edges, no hard rectangle.

A sketch on aged papyrus: an old man's hand with a reed pen and an ink pot of black soot ink, writing the last few lines on a single small sheet, the Greek words ALETHEIA and AGAPE faintly lettered in the margin. Loose ink lines, ochre wash, faded edges blending into the scroll.
